prompt.context: A publishing company has 2 divisions: one that prints SEC disclosures (shareholder communications) and one that prints mutual funds' prospectuses. The company entered the mutual fund prospectus business 10 years ago, and this helped drive revenue growth of 25% over the first 5 years and 15% over the next 5 years. The case is set in 1998.
prompt.question: The CEO wants to know why the rate of revenue growth has slowed and what he can do about it.

clarifying_info.q: What services does the client provide exactly — does it produce content, maintain distribution lists, or solicit firms directly?
clarifying_info.a: The client's services are retained by Investment Banks. When a company needs to access capital markets or make SEC disclosures, it is required by law to send the information to all shareholders. The company uses an Investment Bank to access the markets; the bank gives the information to the client, who prints it and hands it back to the company, which mails it to shareholders. The client does not produce content or maintain its own distribution lists.

clarifying_info.q: What has happened to the client's market share?
Has the Internet affected shareholder communication?
clarifying_info.a: The case is set in 1998, before online shareholder communication was possible. Ignore the effect of the Internet.

clarifying_info.q: Has the quantity of shareholder prospectus booklets printed gone up or down?
clarifying_info.a: The number of booklets printed has gone up.

clarifying_info.q: How does the client charge customers?
clarifying_info.a: The client charges on a per-page basis.

clarifying_info.q: What are the revenues for each division?
clarifying_info.a: Mutual Funds prospectus: $100M in 1988, $300M in 1993, $600M in 1998. Shareholder communications: $500M in 1988, $1B in 1993, $1.7B in 1998.

clarifying_info.q: What caused the number of pages per prospectus to decrease?
clarifying_info.a: In 1993 the SEC mandated the 'easy English usage' rule, which forced companies to reduce legal jargon, thereby reducing the number of pages per prospectus.

clarifying_info.q: What is the competitive landscape like?
clarifying_info.a: There are 3–4 firms offering printing services. There is little differentiation between them. Investment banks switch from one to another based on personality clashes rather than price or service. Prices and service quality are essentially the same across competitors.

clarifying_info.q: Are the client's costs much less than those of the Investment Banks?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, the client's costs are much less than those of the Investment Banks.

clarifying_info.q: Can the client control font size, formatting, or page count?
clarifying_info.a: No. Everything — content, format, and page count — is mandated by the SEC.

framework: Define the revenue driver: R = P × Q; isolate which variable is responsible for slower growth
Split analysis by division: mutual funds prospectus vs. shareholder communications
For each division, assess Price trends, Volume (number of booklets), and Revenue per unit (pages × price per page)
Identify root cause of slowing growth by tracing the gap between rising volume and decelerating revenue
Generate revenue-growth options: (1) raise prices, (2) gain market share, (3) increase pages per document, (4) expand into adjacent markets
Evaluate each option against competitive dynamics, regulatory constraints, and client capabilities

questions.prompt: Walk through the revenue math. Prices are constant and market share is constant — what does that imply about quantity, and does it explain the slowdown?
questions.guidance: Constant prices + constant market share → revenue growth must come from volume. Volume (booklets) has increased, yet revenue growth slowed. This apparent contradiction is resolved by the per-page pricing model: if pages per booklet fell, revenue per booklet fell even as booklet count rose.

math.setup: Revenue = Price per page × Pages per booklet × Number of booklets. With price per page constant and booklets rising, revenue growth slows only if pages per booklet fell.
steps: Mutual Funds prospectus growth 1988–1993: ($300M − $100M)/$100M = 200% over 5 years
Mutual Funds prospectus growth 1993–1998: ($600M − $300M)/$300M = 100% over 5 years
Both divisions decelerated; shareholder communications (larger base) drives most of the absolute slowdown
math.answer: Deceleration is concentrated in the shareholder communications division. The cause is a drop in pages per prospectus — since pricing is per page — not a drop in booklet volume or market share.

questions.prompt: What caused the number of pages per prospectus to decline, and why does that matter for revenue?
questions.guidance: The SEC's 1993 'easy English usage' mandate forced companies to strip out legal jargon, directly reducing page counts. Because the client charges per page, fewer pages per document means lower revenue per document even if the number of documents rises. The client has no control over content or format — both are SEC-mandated — so this is an external structural constraint.

questions.prompt: What options does the client have to raise its revenue growth rate? Evaluate each.
questions.guidance: R = P × Q framework yields four levers: (1) Raise prices — viable because the client's fees are a small fraction of total Investment Bank deal costs; banks switch on personality not price, so modest price increases may not trigger switching; carry out with care given commoditized market. (2) Gain market share — difficult; 3–4 competitors with identical price and service quality, switching driven by relationship not merit. (3) Increase pages per document — ruled out; SEC mandates format and content. (4) Enter adjacent markets — most promising: annual report printing leverages existing relationships with companies and Investment Banks, similar skill set to mutual funds prospectus division; textbook printing is possible but further from core competency. Recommend prioritizing (1) modest price increase and (4) annual report market entry.

brainstorming.prompt: What markets or lines of business could the client expand into to drive revenue growth?

categories.name: Broader corporate communications
ideas: Corporate press releases and IR materials

categories.name: New content verticals
ideas: Legal document printing for law firms

recommendation: Implement a modest price increase — the client's fees are a small fraction of Investment Bank deal costs and banks do not switch on price, making this low-risk

Enter the annual report printing market — it is structurally similar to the mutual funds prospectus business, allows leverage of existing relationships with Investment Banks and corporations, and diversifies the revenue base
risks: Competitors could match a price increase, eroding any gain and triggering a price war
Annual report market may be already served by incumbents with locked-in relationships
Regulatory changes (e.g., future SEC mandates) could further compress page counts or shift format requirements
next_steps: Quantify price elasticity by surveying Investment Bank clients on switching thresholds
Size the annual report printing market and identify the top 5 prospective clients to approach
Assess internal capacity and cost structure to confirm margins on annual report work are attractive
